State Minimum Wage Increases and Low-Wage Employment

A Difference-in-Differences Study with Power, Heterogeneity, and Robustness Analysis

August 26, 2026

Summary

This report estimates the employment effect of the 2021 round of state minimum-wage increases on food service and retail employment, and asks whether that effect scales with pre-policy wage exposure. It follows a pre-specified analysis plan (Section 2 of the project proposal): a headline average-effect result (Model A), a primary scientific hypothesis about exposure heterogeneity (Model C’s β₄, explicitly pre-registered as likely underpowered), and a full confirmatory battery – event study, placebo test, COVID-sensitivity spec, wild cluster bootstrap, and model diagnostics – run before either headline number is taken at face value.

The honest headline: the credibility checks found a real problem, not a clean result. Pre-COVID-era trends between treated and control states were not parallel for food service employment, confirmed by two independent methods (the event study and a simple two-sample t-test), and the entire baseline effect is highly sensitive to how differently states recovered from COVID – a covariate for that alone reduces Model A’s estimated effect by roughly 90%. This is reported as a direct limit on how much weight the average-effect estimate can carry, exactly as the proposal’s own design anticipated it might have to be (Section 6.5).

Identification Strategy

Before any regression equation, the causal logic this design relies on, stated in plain language:

  • Treatment. States with a minimum-wage increase effective in Q1 2021.
  • Comparison. States with no minimum-wage change at all in 2021.
  • Outcome. Quarterly log employment, food service and retail, tracked separately.
  • Counterfactual. Absent the minimum-wage increase, treated states would have followed the same employment trajectory as the comparison states – the parallel-trends assumption every DiD design rests on.
  • Main threat. The 2021 treatment window sits immediately after an extraordinary, unevenly-distributed labor-market shock. If COVID caused states to recover on different trajectories for reasons unrelated to minimum-wage policy, and that difference happens to correlate with treatment status, the counterfactual above fails.
  • Evidence. Three independent checks, run before any DiD coefficient is reported: an event study of the dynamic pre- and post-treatment effects, a joint statistical test of whether the pre-treatment coefficients are consistent with zero, and a COVID-sensitivity specification that directly tests whether differential recovery explains the baseline result.
pretrend <- proc("pretrend_joint_test.csv")

Figure 1 – Pre-treatment trends and dynamic treatment effects

include_graphics(fig("event_study_food_service.png"))

include_graphics(fig("event_study_retail.png"))

The formal joint test that every pre-treatment lead equals zero rejects flat pre-trends for both industries (food service F = 4.77, p < 0.0001; retail F = 3.09, p = 0.001).

Because the pre-treatment coefficients are not jointly consistent with zero, the parallel-trends assumption is not credible for this outcome. Consequently, the baseline DiD coefficient should not be interpreted as a clean causal estimate. Section 4 below tests why directly (a COVID-recovery confound explains a substantial share of it), and Section 9’s Limitations section states this plainly rather than qualifying it away. Every result that follows in this report is presented with that finding already on the table, not as a caveat added at the end.

1. Data and Treatment Classification

Source Role
FRED (public API) State-quarter employment (food service, retail), GDP, population, 2015-2022
U.S. DOL minimum wage history (Wayback Machine snapshots) Treatment classification
QCEW Open Data API Fallback employment series (2 states); wage-ratio validation check
CPS-ORG via IPUMS-CPS Exposure construction (2019-2020 earnings only)

The design compares 20 treated states (raised wages effective 1/1/2021) against 25 control states (source-checked against DOL snapshots from Dec 2020, Feb 2021, and Dec 2021 – confirmed zero minimum-wage movement across all of 2021). A further 5 states raised wages later in 2021 and are excluded from the primary comparison (they aren’t a clean control group for a binary treated indicator).

Two corrections surfaced during data acquisition, both source-verified rather than assumed:

  • Michigan’s 2021 increase never happened. The draft treatment table had it going $9.65 → $9.87; DOL’s own Feb 2021 snapshot still shows $9.65. Michigan’s automatic adjustment is conditioned on the prior year’s unemployment rate staying under 8.5%; the COVID-era spike tripped that clause and the scheduled step was skipped.
  • The control group itself was missing initially. The proposal names the 20 treated and 5 excluded states explicitly but never lists the actual “no 2021 change” control group its own design requires – without it there’s no DiD to run. All 25 remaining states were source-checked and used.
tt <- readr::read_csv("../data/treatment_classification.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tt %>%
  count(group, name = "n_states") %>%
  kable(caption = "State counts by group")
State counts by group
group n_states
control 25
excluded 5
treated 20

2. Exposure Construction

Exposure is the CPS-ORG-weighted share of a state-industry cell’s workers earning within 12.5% of that state’s pre-2021 minimum wage, computed only from 2019-2020 earnings so the post-period outcome can’t contaminate the covariate. The proposal states the band as “10-15%” without picking one number and separately flags band width as a source of construction risk (Section 13); 12.5% (the midpoint) is the primary figure used throughout, with 10% and 15% also computed for sensitivity.

Two validation checks, both passing:

dist_check <- proc("exposure_distribution_check.csv")
qcew_check <- proc("qcew_correlation_check.csv")
  • Exposure-distribution check: food service exposure is higher than retail in 49 of 50 states (mean 0.307 vs. 0.196, Wilcoxon p = 9.93e-10) – the two industries genuinely differ in exposure before that difference is used in Model C.
  • QCEW correlation check: QCEW’s average wage (hourly proxy) over the state minimum wage, correlated against the CPS-ORG exposure share. Both industries show the expected negative relationship (food service r = -0.82, retail r = -0.71) – high-exposure states really do have wages sitting closer to the floor.

4. Credibility Checks

Per Section 6.5 of the proposal, these are presented and interpreted before any DiD coefficient: “the 2021 treatment window follows an extraordinary labor-market shock. This is a central threat to identification… a limit on how much weight the Model A headline number itself can carry if pre-trends look poor.”

4.1 Event Study / Parallel Trends

Dynamic treated × quarter-relative-to-treatment effects, state and quarter fixed effects, state-clustered SEs, 2016 Q1-2022 Q4 (the longest window the growth covariates allow). Shown as Figure 1 in the Identification Strategy section above, ahead of any DiD coefficient; repeated here in a testing context rather than re-embedded.

The pattern isn’t a gradual pre-trend drift so much as a roughly stable, non-zero gap between treated and control states across most of the sample, plus one sharp anomalous dip at quarter -3 relative to treatment – 2020 Q2, the COVID employment trough – most visible in retail.

4.2 Two-Sample t-Test (independent corroboration)

A simpler, STAT-240-level check using a completely different method: compare each state’s raw pre-period (2019 Q1 → 2020 Q4) employment trend between treated and control groups directly, no fixed-effects model involved.

proc("two_sample_ttest_results.csv") %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Two-sample t-test, pre-period trend: treated vs. control")
Two-sample t-test, pre-period trend: treated vs. control
industry mean_treated mean_control t_statistic df p_value ci_low ci_high
food_service -0.1971 -0.1183 3.0259 39.8853 0.0043 0.0262 0.1314
retail -0.0046 0.0066 1.0485 42.7953 0.3003 -0.0103 0.0328

Food service shows a real, significant difference: treated states’ pre-period employment trend was already more negative than control states’ before treatment started (p = 0.0043). This independently confirms the event study’s pre-trend violation with unrelated methodology – not a new problem, the same one caught twice.

4.3 COVID-Sensitivity Specification

Adds covid_severity x post – each state-industry’s log employment change from 2019 Q4 to the 2020 Q2 trough, interacted with the post indicator, since a bare state-constant term would be fully absorbed by the state fixed effect – to Model A and Model C.

covid <- proc("covid_sensitivity_results.csv")
covid %>% kable(digits = 4, caption = "Baseline vs. COVID-sensitivity spec")
Baseline vs. COVID-sensitivity spec
industry model_a_treated_post_baseline model_a_treated_post_covid_spec model_c_beta4_baseline model_c_beta4_covid_spec
food_service -0.025 -0.0021 0.1669 0.0626
retail -0.010 0.0060 -0.0047 0.1018

covid_severity x post is highly significant in every specification (p < 10⁻⁸). Once included, Model A’s treated_post shrinks toward zero (food service: -0.025 → -0.0021) and Model C’s β₄ shifts substantially, even flipping sign for retail (-0.0047 → 0.1018). Differential COVID recovery explains a real share of what the baseline specification below picks up.

4.4 Placebo Test

A false treatment date (2018-01-01), restricted to a pre-COVID window (2016-2019) so it can’t just re-detect the confound already found above.

proc("placebo_test_results.csv") %>% kable(digits = 4, caption = "Placebo test, Model A (beta3), false treatment date 2018-01-01")
Placebo test, Model A (beta3), false treatment date 2018-01-01
industry placebo_date placebo_treated_post placebo_se placebo_p
food_service 2018-01-01 -0.0055 0.0051 0.2917
retail 2018-01-01 -0.0043 0.0054 0.4268

Clean result for the average effect: small, non-significant estimates for both industries. The design doesn’t manufacture a Model A-style effect from nothing when there’s no real policy change to detect – the pre-trend problem above is real and specific to the actual treatment window, not a general flaw in the method.

The same check on Model C’s exposure interaction (β₄, Section 5.2, this report’s primary hypothesis) tells a different story:

proc("placebo_test_beta4_results.csv") %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Placebo test, Model C (beta4), false treatment date 2018-01-01")
Placebo test, Model C (beta4), false treatment date 2018-01-01
industry placebo_date placebo_beta4 placebo_beta4_se placebo_beta4_p
food_service 2018-01-01 0.1113 0.0257 0.0001
retail 2018-01-01 0.0640 0.0256 0.0164

Both industries come back significant at the fake date (food service p < 0.001, retail p = 0.016) – the opposite of the clean Model A result above. This means states with higher pre-2021 exposure already had systematically different employment trends in 2016-2019, for reasons that have nothing to do with the real 2021 minimum-wage increases. Since that same exposure measure is what the real Model C relies on to identify β₄, this is a direct threat to the exposure-gradient result’s credibility specifically – not just a general caveat, but evidence that part of what Section 5.2’s β₄ estimate is picking up may be a pre-existing structural difference between high- and low-exposure states rather than a treatment effect. Combined with Section 6.3’s specification curve, this is the second independent piece of evidence that the exposure-gradient result should not be read as clean causal evidence.

5. Core Confirmatory Results

Given Section 4 above, these are reported with the caveat already attached, not as a clean average effect. All four confirmatory estimates, at a glance, before the specification-by-specification detail:

include_graphics(fig("coefficient_forest_plot.png"))

5.1 Model A – Headline Average Effect (β₃)

Two-way fixed-effects DiD: log_employment ~ treated_post + gdp_growth + pop_growth | state + quarter, state-clustered SEs, treated + control states only.

mac <- proc("model_a_c_results.csv")
mac %>%
  select(sample, industry, model_a_treated_post, model_a_se, model_a_p) %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Model A: treated_post coefficient")
Model A: treated_post coefficient
sample industry model_a_treated_post model_a_se model_a_p
full 20-state treated sample food_service -0.0250 0.0157 0.1179
full 20-state treated sample retail -0.0100 0.0114 0.3853
>=$0.50-increase subsample food_service -0.0475 0.0188 0.0162
>=$0.50-increase subsample retail -0.0274 0.0134 0.0486

Negative in all 4 specifications, but only significant in the ≥$0.50-increase subsample (food service p = 0.016, retail p = 0.049) – the full sample is diluted by treated states whose increases were as small as $0.00-0.19. Every fixest estimate was cross-checked against an independent lm() + sandwich::vcovCL() fit; coefficients and clustered SEs matched to 4+ decimal places in all 4 specifications.

5.2 Model C – Exposure Interaction (β₄, primary scientific hypothesis)

mac %>%
  select(sample, industry, model_c_beta4_treated_post_x_exposure, model_c_beta4_se, model_c_beta4_p) %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Model C: beta4 (treated_post x exposure)")
Model C: beta4 (treated_post x exposure)
sample industry model_c_beta4_treated_post_x_exposure model_c_beta4_se model_c_beta4_p
full 20-state treated sample food_service 0.1669 0.1724 0.3384
full 20-state treated sample retail -0.0047 0.0796 0.9530
>=$0.50-increase subsample food_service 0.4186 0.2264 0.0731
>=$0.50-increase subsample retail -0.2965 0.1205 0.0191

Noisy and sign-inconsistent across specifications – positive for food service, negative for retail, significant only in the ≥$0.50 subsample. Section 4.4 of the proposal pre-registers this exact possibility: the design may not reliably distinguish “no gradient” from “real gradient” given the sample size. A noisy β₄ is a valid, expected outcome under that pre-registration, not a failed analysis.

5.3 Coefficient Interpretation

Neither coefficient is self-explanatory from the table alone, so spelled out explicitly:

  • Model A (β₃). The full-sample food-service estimate is -0.025 – because the outcome is log employment, this corresponds to an approximately 2.5% lower employment level for treated states relative to control states after the 2021 increase, holding GDP growth, population growth, and the state/quarter fixed effects constant. It is not a dollar figure, a job count, or a percentage-point change in an employment rate – purely a relative log-scale gap between the two groups.
  • Model C (β₄). β₄ measures how the estimated treatment effect itself changes as a state-industry’s pre-treatment exposure share increases – formally, ∂(treatment effect)/∂(exposure) = β₄. A positive β₄ (food service, this report) means the treatment effect becomes more positive as exposure rises; a negative β₄ (retail) means it becomes more negative. β₄ is not itself an employment effect – it’s the slope of the employment effect with respect to exposure, which is why Section 5.4 plots it as a curve rather than a single number.

5.4 Marginal Effect of Treatment by Exposure Level

include_graphics(fig("marginal_effects.png"))

This is Model C’s practical content: the estimated treatment effect (β₃ + β₄ × exposure) across the actual range of pre-2021 exposure observed, with a 95% confidence band from the model’s clustered variance-covariance matrix (delta method). Food service’s line has a visible upward slope – higher-exposure states show a smaller (less-negative) estimated effect – while retail’s is nearly flat. The band’s width, not just its slope, is the point: it comfortably contains zero across the entire exposure range for both industries, which is the same underpowering conclusion Section 7.5’s formal power analysis reaches by simulation instead of visually.

5.5 Exposure Bandwidth Sensitivity

Is β₄ an artifact of the arbitrary 12.5% exposure-band choice? Model C refit at the two alternative bandwidths R/04 already computes (10%, 15%) but never previously used downstream:

bw <- proc("exposure_bandwidth_sensitivity.csv")
bw %>%
  select(bandwidth, industry, beta4, beta4_se, beta4_p) %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Model C beta4 across exposure bandwidths")
Model C beta4 across exposure bandwidths
bandwidth industry beta4 beta4_se beta4_p
10% food_service 0.2066 0.1295 0.1177
12.5% food_service 0.1669 0.1724 0.3384
15% food_service 0.1086 0.1921 0.5748
10% retail -0.0146 0.0898 0.8715
12.5% retail -0.0047 0.0796 0.9530
15% retail -0.0194 0.0806 0.8107

Food service stays positive and never significant across all three bandwidths; retail stays small and never significant, though its sign flips between the 10% band and the wider two. Nothing here overturns Section 5.2’s conclusion – the result is not an artifact of picking 12.5% specifically, but it was never precise enough to distinguish a real gradient from noise at any of the three definitions either.

5.6 Leave-One-State-Out Sensitivity

Is Model A’s estimate driven by any single treated state? Section 6.2’s model diagnostics already flag Vermont, New York, and Hawaii as high-leverage (2020 Q2-Q3 observations) – this checks what actually happens to the coefficient, not just the leverage diagnostic, refitting Model A once per treated state with that state dropped entirely.

include_graphics(fig("leave_one_out.png"))

loo <- proc("leave_one_out_results.csv")
loo %>%
  group_by(industry) %>%
  summarise(min_estimate = min(treated_post), max_estimate = max(treated_post)) %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Range of treated_post across all 20 single-state exclusions")
Range of treated_post across all 20 single-state exclusions
industry min_estimate max_estimate
food_service -0.0311 -0.0213
retail -0.0141 -0.0066

The estimate stays negative and moves only modestly regardless of which state is dropped, for both industries – reassuring on its own terms, though it doesn’t touch the pre-trend violation or COVID confound already established above.

6. Robustness

6.1 Wild Cluster Bootstrap for β₃ and β₄

fwildclusterboot, the standard package for this, was archived by CRAN in 2024 and doesn’t build on current R, so the Cameron-Gelbach-Miller procedure (999 Rademacher-weight replications on the restricted-model residuals) is implemented directly, for both coefficients – the proposal’s Section 8 only specified β₄, but the same low-cluster-count concern applies equally to β₃.

proc("cluster_bootstrap_results.csv") %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Wild cluster bootstrap, beta4 (full 20-treated-state sample)")
Wild cluster bootstrap, beta4 (full 20-treated-state sample)
industry beta4 beta4_se_asymptotic beta4_t_asymptotic wild_boot_p_value wild_boot_ci_low wild_boot_ci_high
food_service 0.1669 0.1724 0.9678 0.3674 -0.1921 0.5383
retail -0.0047 0.0796 -0.0593 0.9530 -0.1829 0.1721 
proc("cluster_bootstrap_beta3_results.csv") %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Wild cluster bootstrap, beta3 (full 20-treated-state sample)")
Wild cluster bootstrap, beta3 (full 20-treated-state sample)
industry beta3 beta3_se_asymptotic beta3_t_asymptotic wild_boot_p_value wild_boot_ci_low wild_boot_ci_high
food_service -0.025 0.0157 -1.5948 0.1071 -0.0560 0.0062
retail -0.010 0.0114 -0.8770 0.3874 -0.0339 0.0124

Bootstrap p-values track the asymptotic ones closely for both coefficients (β₄: food service 0.367 vs. 0.338 asymptotic, retail 0.953 vs. 0.953; β₃: food service 0.107 vs. 0.118 asymptotic, retail 0.387 vs. 0.385) – confirms rather than overturns the Model A and Model C results above, under an inference method built specifically for this few clusters.

6.2 Model Diagnostics

proc("model_diagnostics_summary.csv") %>% kable(digits = 4, caption = "Model A diagnostics summary")
Model A diagnostics summary

include_graphics(fig("model_a_diagnostics_food_service.png"))

include_graphics(fig("model_a_diagnostics_retail.png"))

Residuals are non-normal by Shapiro-Wilk (though that test is hypersensitive with 1,260 observations). More informative: the specific highest-leverage points in both industries are 2020 Q2-Q3 observations – Vermont and New York (Q2 2020), Hawaii (Q3 2020, heavily tourism-dependent) – the same COVID window Section 4 already identified, not a separate data problem. No single observation is extreme by Cook’s distance.

6.3 Specification Curve

Sections 5.5 and this report’s sample cut each vary one analytical choice against β₄ in isolation – exposure bandwidth alone, or the full-vs-subsample cut alone. A specification curve varies every combination of both, together with industry, in one view: 3 exposure bands x 2 samples x 2 industries = 12 specifications, all estimating the same β₄ hypothesis.

proc("specification_curve.csv") %>%
  select(bandwidth, sample, industry, beta4, se, p_value, significant) %>%
  arrange(desc(beta4)) %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "beta4 across all 12 specifications")
beta4 across all 12 specifications

15% >=$0.50 subsample food_service 0.3920 0.2590 0.1394 FALSE
10% full 20-state sample food_service 0.2066 0.1295 0.1177 FALSE
10% >=$0.50 subsample food_service 0.1783 0.1653 0.2884 FALSE
12.5% full 20-state sample food_service 0.1669 0.1724 0.3384 FALSE
15% full 20-state sample food_service 0.1086 0.1921 0.5748 FALSE
12.5% full 20-state sample retail -0.0047 0.0796 0.9530 FALSE
10% full 20-state sample retail -0.0146 0.0898 0.8715 FALSE
15% full 20-state sample retail -0.0194 0.0806 0.8107 FALSE

include_graphics(fig("specification_curve.png"))

Only 2 of the 12 specifications are significant at p < 0.05, and both are retail under the >=$0.50 subsample – the same subsample already flagged in Section 5.1 as the only place Model A reaches significance. Food service is never significant in any of the 6 specifications that use it, and its point estimate is positive in all 6 while retail’s is negative in all 6 – the two industries don’t even agree on sign. This is the clearest single piece of evidence in the report that the exposure-gradient result is fragile to analytical choices rather than a stable feature of the data.

7. Exploratory Analyses

These inform the picture but don’t validate or override the confirmatory results above (Section 12 of the proposal).

7.1 SLR and MLR (STAT 240/340 coursework closure)

Simple pre/post comparisons, not the study’s identification strategy. SLR: log employment change (2019-2020 → 2021-2022) on the dollar size of the wage increase, treated states only – not significant for either industry (food service p = 0.46, retail p = 0.62).

include_graphics(fig("slr_log_change_food_service_scatter.png"))

include_graphics(fig("slr_log_change_retail_scatter.png"))

MLR: adds treatment status, GDP growth, population growth, and Census region, treated + control states. The treated coefficient is null for both industries (food service p = 0.65, retail p = 0.26) – an earlier version of this model that accidentally included the contaminated “excluded” group as a stand-in control showed a marginally significant result for food service; that turned out to be an artifact of the contamination, not a real signal, corrected once the real control group was built.

7.2 Regional ANOVA – exploratory regional variation in employment growth, not a treatment-effect estimate

This uses the full sample – treated, excluded, and control states together – as a general regional comparison, not a causal test of minimum-wage policy. Labeled explicitly here so it isn’t mistaken for another heterogeneity check on the treatment itself: that’s Model C (Section 5.2), the formal test.

proc("regional_anova_results.csv") %>% kable(digits = 4, caption = "One-way ANOVA: log employment change ~ Census region")
One-way ANOVA: log employment change ~ Census region
outcome f_statistic df_region df_residuals p_value

log_change_retail 5.6414 3 46 0.0022 
include_graphics(fig("regional_boxplot_log_change_food_service.png"))

include_graphics(fig("regional_boxplot_log_change_retail.png"))

Regions differ significantly in employment growth for both industries (West notably higher than Midwest/South) – real geographic heterogeneity, unrelated to treatment. The exposure interaction in Model C remains the formal heterogeneity test; this is exploratory only.

10,000 relabelings of which states are “treated” (state-level, holding n_treated fixed at 20), Model A refit each time.

Permutation p-values track the asymptotic Model A p-values closely (food service 0.09 vs. 0.118; retail 0.377 vs. 0.385) – another confirmation of the Model A result via a completely different inferential route.

Post-build addition: this section originally covered Model A only. The same relabeling exercise applies to Model C’s exposure interaction (β₄, Section 5.2, the primary scientific hypothesis) – each replication keeps every state’s own exposure value fixed and only randomizes which states count as “treated,” the same logic as the Model A version above.

proc("permutation_test_beta4_results.csv") %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Permutation test, Model C (beta4) treated_post:exposure")
Permutation test, Model C (beta4) treated_post:exposure
industry observed_beta4 null_mean null_sd permutation_p_value
food_service 0.1669 -0.0872 0.0617 0.1001
retail -0.0047 -0.0767 0.0586 0.9717 
include_graphics(fig("permutation_test_beta4_food_service.png"))

include_graphics(fig("permutation_test_beta4_retail.png"))

Retail’s permutation p-value (0.972) tracks its asymptotic one (0.953) about as closely as Model A’s do. Food service’s don’t: permutation p = 0.100 versus an asymptotic p = 0.338 – more than a 3x difference, though neither crosses the conventional 0.05 threshold. The reason is visible in the null distribution itself: its mean is -0.087, not approximately zero the way Model A’s permutation null is (0.00001). Reassigning which states are “treated” while leaving each state’s real, fixed exposure value in place produces a systematically negative placebo β₄ on average – exactly the kind of exposure-linked, treatment-unrelated structure Section 4.4’s placebo test already found at a false date. This is now the third independent check (with the specification curve and the placebo test) pointing at the same underlying issue: part of what looks like an exposure gradient in this data may be a pre-existing association between exposure and employment trends, not a treatment effect.

7.4 Power Analysis for β₃ (Model A average effect, added after the original build)

Section 4.4 specifies two power analyses, not one: average-effect power for β₃ at assumed sizes of 0.5%, 1%, 2%, and 3%, reporting the minimum detectable effect (MDE); and a separate heterogeneity-detection power analysis for β₄ (Section 7.5). Both were added after the original 10-day build (R/16_power_analysis.R; see TIMELINE.md).

proc("power_analysis_beta3_results.csv") %>% kable(digits = 4, caption = "Observed beta3 vs. minimum detectable effect at 80% power, Section 4.4's assumed grid (0.5%-3%)")
Observed beta3 vs. minimum detectable effect at 80% power, Section 4.4’s assumed grid (0.5%-3%)
industry observed_beta3 mde_80
food_service -0.025 NA
retail -0.010 NA 
include_graphics(fig("power_analysis_beta3.png"))

The MDE isn’t reached anywhere in Section 4.4’s own assumed range for either industry – the design needs a true average effect larger than 3% before it reliably clears 80% power. That’s consistent with the rest of this report: Model A only came back significant in the ≥$0.50-increase subsample (Section 5.1). Food service’s estimate there (4.75%) is comfortably past the range this grid covers; retail’s (2.74%) sits inside it and only barely cleared significance (p = 0.049) – exactly what falling short of 80% power in that region would predict, a real but not guaranteed chance of detecting it. The full 20-state sample’s smaller, more diluted average effect never had a realistic shot at significance given this design’s power.

7.5 Power Analysis for β₄ (exposure gradient, added after the original build)

The exposure-gradient hypothesis (β₄) was separately pre-registered as likely underpowered (Section 4.4’s heterogeneity-detection question). The quantitative version – a residual-based Monte Carlo power simulation on the real panel – makes that concrete.

proc("power_analysis_results.csv") %>% kable(digits = 3, caption = "Observed beta4 vs. minimum detectable effect at 80% power")
Observed beta4 vs. minimum detectable effect at 80% power
industry observed_beta4 mde_80
food_service 0.167 0.50
retail -0.005 0.22 
include_graphics(fig("power_analysis.png"))

Both industries’ observed β₄ estimates fall well short of their own minimum detectable effect at 80% power – the design would need a true exposure gradient roughly 3x (retail) to 5x (food service) larger than what was actually estimated before it could reliably distinguish that effect from noise. This is consistent with, and quantifies, the qualitative pre-registered expectation. The simulation quantifies which effect sizes this design could realistically distinguish from zero – it is a design property, not a way of explaining away the noisy β₄ result above after the fact.

7.6 Exploratory Treatment-Intensity Model

Exploratory, not confirmatory – not part of the six-check confirmatory family in Section 8. The dollar size of a state’s increase is not randomly assigned; states that raised wages by $1.00 vs. $0.08 may differ systematically in ways unrelated to the policy itself. With that caveat: does a larger increase correspond to a larger employment response, rather than a simple treated/not-treated split?

proc("treatment_intensity_results.csv") %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Exploratory: log employment ~ (wage increase x post), continuous dollar amount")
Exploratory: log employment ~ (wage increase x post), continuous dollar amount
industry beta1_wage_increase_post beta1_se beta1_p
food_service -0.0358 0.0172 0.0429
retail -0.0196 0.0140 0.1689

Food service’s coefficient is negative and marginally significant (p = 0.04); retail’s is negative but not significant. Directionally consistent with Model A’s binary result, but given the non-random assignment of increase size, this doesn’t upgrade the evidence – it’s one more piece of exploratory information, not a sharper confirmatory estimate.

8. Multiple Testing and Inferential Hierarchy

Two things are true at once in this report, and they’re not in tension: Model A (Section 5.1, β₃) is the headline result, and β₄ (Section 5.2) is the primary scientific hypothesis. They answer different questions – “is there an average effect” versus “does it vary with exposure” – and one is never substituted for the other. Model A is reported first because it’s the best-powered result (Section 7.4 quantifies exactly how well-powered); β₄ is reported alongside its own power ceiling (Section 7.5) rather than read as a clean null just because it came back noisy.

The confirmatory family is small and explicit, fixed before any model was run rather than assembled after seeing results: Model A and Model C for both industries (Sections 5.1, 5.2), the event study (Section 4.1), the exposure-measurement validation (Section 2), both power analyses (Sections 7.4, 7.5), the wild cluster bootstrap (Section 6.1), and the placebo/COVID-sensitivity checks (Sections 4.3, 4.4). This family is what determines the headline claim.

The regional ANOVA (Section 7.2), the SLR/MLR coursework-closure pieces (Section 7.1), and the Monte Carlo permutation test (Section 7.3) are exploratory. They inform the picture – the permutation test in particular corroborates Model A from a distribution-free angle – but none of them validate or overturn the confirmatory family’s result, and none are treated as if they could.

Naming the confirmatory family also means it can be corrected for formally, not just described narratively. Holm-adjusted p-values across the 4 primary tests (β₃ and β₄, both industries, headline specification):

proc("multiple_testing_correction.csv") %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Holm-adjusted p-values, confirmatory family")
Holm-adjusted p-values, confirmatory family
coefficient industry p_raw p_holm
beta3 food_service 0.1179 0.4717
beta3 retail 0.3853 1.0000
beta4 food_service 0.3384 1.0000
beta4 retail 0.9530 1.0000

None of the 4 survive correction at the headline specification – the same conclusion Sections 5 and 7 already reach individually, now stated as a formal joint test rather than four separate uncorrected p-values that happen to agree.

9. Limitations

  • Non-random policy adoption; parallel trends is a tested assumption, not a proven one, and Section 4 above shows it doesn’t fully hold for food service.
  • COVID confound: the single largest limitation this analysis found. A meaningful share of the baseline effect is attributable to differential COVID recovery, not minimum wage policy.
  • Limited power, for both β₃ and β₄ – pre-registered in Section 4.4 of the proposal as a qualitative expectation for both, and borne out by the actual results. The formal quantitative piece for both was scoped out of the original 10-day build, but was added afterward (R/16_power_analysis.R, a residual-based Monte Carlo simulation on the real panel). For β₄: the minimum detectable effect at 80% power is β₄≈0.50 for food service and β₄≈0.22 for retail, both well above the actual observed estimates (0.167 and -0.005). For β₃ (Model A, Section 7.4): the MDE isn’t reached anywhere in the proposal’s own assumed 0.5%-3% range for either industry – consistent with Model A’s significant results only showing up in the ≥$0.50-increase subsample, where the estimated effects are large enough to fall in or past that range. The qualitative pre-registration held up for both parameters, and the numbers that would have quantified it going in now exist too.
  • Exposure-measure construction risk: band width (10-15%) and cell pooling rules are documented choices, not the only defensible ones.
  • The exposure-gradient placebo test fails (Section 4.4): at a false 2018 treatment date, the exposure-interaction term is significant for both industries, meaning high- and low-exposure states already had different employment trends before 2021 for reasons unrelated to the real policy. This directly threatens β₄’s identification specifically – part of the real estimate may reflect this pre-existing structural difference rather than a treatment effect, consistent with Section 6.3’s specification curve showing the same result is fragile to sample and industry choice. Section 7.3’s permutation test corroborates this from a third, unrelated angle: its placebo null distribution for β₄ isn’t centered at zero for food service (mean -0.087) the way Model A’s permutation null is – reassigning treatment labels while keeping each state’s real exposure value fixed produces a systematically negative “effect” on average, the same pattern the placebo test found.
  • Multi-change states excluded from the primary comparison. The conflation of small legislated increases with automatic CPI adjustments turns out not to be separable at all in this data, not just “only partially addressed”: the ≥$0.50-increase subsample and the legislated-only subsample are the exact same 10 states (confirmed in data/processed/model_a_c_results.csv’s n_legislated_treated column), so the dollar-threshold cut and the mechanism cut can’t be disentangled here – any difference attributed to “legislated vs. automatic” in this sample is equally attributable to “large vs. small.”
  • ~20-45 clusters: addressed via state-clustered SEs throughout and the wild cluster bootstrap for β₄, but inference with this few clusters always carries some caution.
  • Spillovers between neighboring states aren’t modeled – a control state bordering several treated states could see labor migrate or employers adjust in anticipation, which would bias the control group’s outcome toward the treatment effect (attenuating the estimate) rather than leaving it a clean counterfactual.
  • Anticipation effects: employers and workers may have responded ahead of the 1/1/2021 effective date once increases were signed into law or scheduled, which the binary treated/post cutoff doesn’t capture.
  • External validity: this window is COVID-era by construction: even setting the COVID-sensitivity confound (above) aside, an estimate from 2019-2022 may not generalize to a minimum-wage increase in a more typical labor market.
  • The permutation test (Section 7.3) is a reference distribution, not evidence of a randomized experiment. States chose whether and when to raise wages; permuting treatment labels tests statistical extremeness against a null of no effect, not against a null of “as-if-random” assignment, since the assignment was never random to begin with.

10. Conclusion

The working hypothesis going in was a small average effect with an inconclusive exposure gradient, reported honestly regardless of significance (Section 15 of the proposal). That’s what happened, plus something the proposal explicitly built the credibility-check infrastructure to catch: a real, COVID-driven confound that meaningfully changes how much weight the headline estimate can carry. Success here isn’t a clean significant result – it’s that the event study, two-sample t-test, placebo test, and COVID-sensitivity spec did their jobs and surfaced a real problem before it could be reported as a clean finding. The quantitative power simulation added after the original build (Section 9) independently confirms the same story: the design is underpowered for β₄ at the effect sizes actually observed, not just in the qualitative pre-registered expectation.

Reproducibility: every number and figure in this report is generated by R/01_treatment_classification.R through R/15_permutation_test.R, run in order, from min-wage-difference-in-differences-study’s repo root. See README.md and TIMELINE.md for the day-by-day build log, including every defect found and corrected along the way.
